## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of real-world CPU resource management, cgroup behavior, and observability under bursts. It requires using default tools to diagnose throttling, map it to a specific process, and apply a conservative fix without destabilizing other workloads.

## Key Concepts
- Cgroup CPU quotas and throttling
- Process-level visibility under bursts
- Safe isolation and re-observation

## Code Example
```bash
# 1) Identify quotas
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/<slice>/cpu.cfs_quota_us
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/<slice>/cpu.cfs_period_us
# 2) Find contending processes
pidstat -p ALL 1
# 3) Mitigate
echo 200000 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/<slice>/cpu.cfs_quota_us
taskset -pc 0-3 <pid>
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle v2 unified cgroups differently?
- What metrics would you monitor to ensure no regressions after mitigation?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests deep, OS-level debugging skills for memory pressure in containerized workloads using only default Linux tools. It demonstrates a candidate's ability to diagnose root causes, map memory behavior to specific containers, and apply safe mitigations without relying on external profilers or commercial tooling.

## Key Concepts
- **Memory reclaim and fragmentation**: Tools like buddyinfo, slabtop, and meminfo reveal allocator behavior and page availability
- **cgroups memory accounting**: memory.stat and RSS mapping via /proc/[pid]/cgroup link container processes to memory consumption
- **Transparent huge pages**: Can introduce latency spikes when defragmentation triggers during memory pressure
- **vm.min_free_kbytes**: Reserves memory to prevent OOM conditions and reduce reclaim latency
